title: Find in a Rotated List with Repeats
statement:
An array was sorted in non-decreasing order and then rotated: some suffix was cut off and moved to the front. So [1, 2, 2, 5, 7] might now read [5, 7, 1, 2, 2]. The rotation may also be zero. Unlike the plain version of this problem, values can repeat.

Return true if target appears in nums, otherwise false.

Aim to discard as much of the array per step as you can. Explain why repeats make an O(log n) guarantee impossible in the worst case.

examples.why: The 2 sits in the part that was rotated behind the 6s.
The first, middle and last values are all 3, so they don't show which half is sorted. A search that guesses "the left half is sorted" throws the 1 away.
3 is between 0 and 4 but is not in the array.

constraints: nums is a rotation of a non-decreasing array
hints: In the version without repeats, comparing nums[lo] with nums[mid] tells you which half is sorted. When does that comparison stop telling you anything?
If nums[lo], nums[mid] and nums[hi] are all equal, the rotation point could be on either side. You can't pick a half, but you can still make safe progress.
When all three are equal and none is the target, drop both ends: lo++ and hi−−. They equal nums[mid], which is not the target, so nothing is lost. Otherwise run the usual sorted-half logic.

explain.intuition:
Any window [lo, hi] of a rotated sorted array splits at mid into two halves, and at least one of them is sorted. Without repeats, nums[lo] ≤ nums[mid] proves the left half is sorted. Then you check whether the target falls inside that half's range and throw away the other half.

Repeats break this in one situation only: nums[lo] == nums[mid] == nums[hi]. In [3, 1, 3, 3, 3] the dip is on the left; in [3, 3, 3, 1, 3] it is on the right. Both look the same from those three spots. You can still shrink the window safely, because nums[lo] and nums[hi] equal nums[mid], which you already know is not the target. On an array like [1, 1, 1, …, 1, 2, 1, 1] you may shrink one step at a time, so the worst case is O(n). On most inputs it is still logarithmic.
steps: If nums[lo] == nums[mid] == nums[hi], do lo++ and hi−− and continue.
Else if nums[lo] ≤ nums[mid], the left half is sorted: if nums[lo] ≤ target < nums[mid], set hi = mid − 1, otherwise lo = mid + 1.
Else the right half is sorted: if nums[mid] < target ≤ nums[hi], set lo = mid + 1, otherwise hi = mid − 1.
pitfalls: Reusing the no-repeats code as is. On [3, 1, 3, 3, 3] it decides the left half is sorted, sees that 1 is outside [3, 3), and drops the half that holds the 1.
Shrinking only when nums[lo] == nums[mid] without checking nums[hi]. That works, but it gives up a valid sorted-half decision in cases like [2, 2, 2, 3, 1], where the left half really is sorted.
Claiming O(log n) in the interview. With repeats, no method can beat O(n) in the worst case: in an array of all 1s with one 2, every unchecked spot could hide the 2.

complexity.time: O(log n) typical, O(n) worst case

solutions.title: Linear scan
solutions.idea: Check every value. With repeats the worst case is O(n) anyway, so this is a fair baseline to mention first.

solutions.title: Binary search that shrinks on ties
solutions.idea: Use the sorted half to discard half the window. When the first, middle and last values are equal, you can't tell which half is sorted, so drop both ends instead.

followups: Return the index of the rotation point (the smallest value) instead. How do ties change that search?
If you knew the array had at most a few repeated values, could you get back an O(log n) guarantee?
